citations.quote:
The Cook condition is
that $t\mapsto\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is norm-$C^1$ on
$[1,\infty)$ and, for constants $C_{\eta,f}\ge0$ and
$\epsilon_{\eta,f}>0$,
$$\left\|\frac{d}{dt}\Psi_t^\eta(f)\right\|\le C_{\eta,f}(1+t)^{-1-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\qquad(t\ge1).$$

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
Fix $1\le s\le t$. If $s=t$ the increment inequality is immediate.
If $s<t$, restrict $r\mapsto\Psi_r^\eta(f)$ to $[s,t]$. By [F1] this is a
continuous curve into the Banach space $\mathcal H$, differentiable on $(s,t)$
with derivative extending continuously to $[s,t]$.
The contract's Countable Choice premise satisfies the hypothesis of [F3], so
the Banach-valued fundamental theorem gives
$\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)=\int_s^t\partial_r\Psi_r^\eta(f)\,dr$.
The derivative is continuous and hence Bochner integrable on this compact
interval; [F4] then gives
$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)\|\le\int_s^t
\|\partial_r\Psi_r^\eta(f)\|\,dr$.

Apply the derivative bound in [F1] and integrate the scalar power:
$$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)\|\le \frac{C_{\eta,f}}{\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\bigl((1+s)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}-(1+t)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\bigr)\le \frac{C_{\eta,f}}{\epsilon_{\eta,f}}(1+s)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}.$$
As $s\to\infty$, the last expression tends to zero uniformly for $t\ge s$.
Thus $\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is Cauchy as $t\to\infty$; completeness gives a limit
$W_\eta f\in\mathcal H$. Taking $t\to\infty$ in the first inequality gives
the claimed rate, and taking $s=1$ gives
$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)\|\le\|\Psi_1^\eta(f)\|+
C_{\eta,f}/\epsilon_{\eta,f}$ for every $t\ge1$.

For $f,g\in\mathcal D_\sigma$, linearity of each $\Psi_t^\eta$ and norm
convergence from 2.1 imply
$W_\eta(af+bg)=aW_\eta f+bW_\eta g$ for all scalars $a,b\in\mathbb C$:
apply the triangle inequality to the finite linear combination and pass to
the limit. Hence $W_\eta$ is linear on $\mathcal D_\sigma$.

By continuity of the Hilbert inner product and the assumed limit [A1],
$(W_\eta f,W_\eta g)=\lim_{t\to\infty}
(\Psi_t^\eta(f),\Psi_t^\eta(g))=(f,g)_{\mathcal F,1}$.
Setting $g=f$ proves preservation of norm, so $W_\eta$ is an isometry on
$\mathcal D_\sigma$.

If $(f_n)$ in $\mathcal D_\sigma$ converges in its Hilbert-space closure,
then $(W_\eta f_n)$ is Cauchy because
$\|W_\eta f_n-W_\eta f_k\|=\|f_n-f_k\|$. Completeness of $\mathcal H$
defines a limit independent of the approximating sequence; the same equality
passes to the limit. This is the unique isometric extension to
$\overline{\mathcal D_\sigma}$. No surjectivity onto $\mathcal H$ follows.

derivations.claim:
By [F3], the bounded linear isometry $\Omega_+$ has a bounded Hilbert
adjoint. For any $z$ in a Hilbert space,
$\|z\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(z,x)|$: Cauchy–Schwarz gives the upper bound, and
if $z\ne0$ the choice $x=z/\|z\|$ attains it. For $y\in\mathcal H$, the
adjoint identity and [F2] therefore give
$\|\Omega_+^*y\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(\Omega_+^*y,x)|
=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(y,\Omega_+x)|\le\|y\|$, since $\|\Omega_+x\|=\|x\|$.
Therefore
$\|Sx\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|\le\|\Omega_-x\|=\|x\|$ for every
$x\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$, so $S$ is a contraction.

By [F3], the bounded maps $\Omega_\pm$ and $S$ have bounded Hilbert
adjoints with the stated adjoint identities. For either isometry $\Omega$,
the adjoint identity gives
$(x,\Omega^*\Omega y)=(\Omega x,\Omega y)=(x,y)$ for all $x,y$; nondegeneracy
therefore gives $\Omega^*\Omega=I$. For $P=\Omega\Omega^*$ the same identity
gives $(Px,y)=(\Omega^*x,\Omega^*y)=(x,Py)$, so $P^*=P$, and
$\Omega^*\Omega=I$ gives $P^2=P$. Also $P$ fixes each $\Omega x$ and its
image is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}\Omega$, so $P$ is the orthogonal
projection onto the closed range. If
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-=:R$, both products
are the same projection $P_R$. For all $x,z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$,
$(Sx,z)_{\mathrm{as}}=(\Omega_-x,\Omega_+z)_{\mathcal H}
=(x,\Omega_-^*\Omega_+z)_{\mathrm{as}}$, so uniqueness of the adjoint gives
$S^*=\Omega_-^*\Omega_+$. It follows that
$S^*S=\Omega_-^*P_R\Omega_-=\Omega_-^*\Omega_-=I$ and
$SS^*=\Omega_+^*P_R\Omega_+=\Omega_+^*\Omega_+=I$, so $S$ is unitary.

Conversely, suppose $S$ is unitary and put
$P_+=\Omega_+\Omega_+^*$. By [F3] and step 1.2 this is a bounded
orthogonal projection.
For each $x$,
$\|P_+\Omega_-x\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|=\|Sx\|=\|x\|
=\|\Omega_-x\|$. For an orthogonal projection $P$, the identity
$\|Py\|=\|y\|$ implies
$\|y\|^2=\|Py\|^2+\|(I-P)y\|^2$ and hence $(I-P)y=0$; therefore
$\Omega_-x\in\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$ for every $x$, proving
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$. Since $S$
is onto, for every $z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$ choose $x$ with $Sx=z$.
Then $\Omega_+z=\Omega_+Sx=P_+\Omega_-x=\Omega_-x$, which gives the reverse
range inclusion. Thus the ranges coincide.

derivations.claim:
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$(\Omega_-(z),\Omega_-(w))=z\overline w=(z,w)$ and
$(\Omega_+(z),\Omega_+(w))=z\overline w=(z,w)$ in the standard
first-variable-linear inner products, so both maps are isometries.
Their ranges are $\mathbb C\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb C$,
respectively, and are distinct proper subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$.

The Hilbert adjoint is $\Omega_+^*(x,y)=y$, since
$(\Omega_+z,(x,y))=(z,y)$ for all $z,x,y$. Hence
$\Omega_+^*\Omega_-(z)=\Omega_+^*(z,0)=0$ for every $z$. The zero map is
not unitary because it does not preserve the norm of $1\in\mathbb C$ and is
not surjective. This refutes the unqualified claim and shows that isometry
and limit existence do not imply full asymptotic completeness.
